claim: The hippocampus has been proposed to encode environments using a representation that contains predictive information about likely future states, called the successor representation.
source: The hippocampus has been proposed to encode environments using a representation that contains predictive information about likely future states, called the successor representation.
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical proposal in the field, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The proposed plasticity rule can learn the predictive map of the environment using a spiking neural network.
source: Here, we propose a plasticity rule that can learn this predictive map of the environment using a spiking neural network.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the mathematical derivations and simulations presented.

claim: The biologically plausible plasticity rule implements the TD-lambda algorithm.
source: We connect this biologically plausible plasticity rule to reinforcement learning, mathematically and numerically showing that it implements the TD-lambda algorithm.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical derivations in the Appendix and numerical simulations.

claim: The framework naturally encompasses behavioral activity and replays.
source: By spanning these different levels, we show how our framework naturally encompasses behavioral activity and replays, smoothly moving from rate to temporal coding, and allows learning over behavioral timescales with a plasticity rule acting on a timescale of milliseconds.
evidence: This is supported by the mathematical analysis showing how different timescales correspond to different values of lambda.

claim: The framework allows learning over behavioral timescales with a plasticity rule acting on a timescale of milliseconds.
source: By spanning these different levels, we show how our framework naturally encompasses behavioral activity and replays, smoothly moving from rate to temporal coding, and allows learning over behavioral timescales with a plasticity rule acting on a timescale of milliseconds.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the bootstrapping property of TD learning as explained in the Results section.

claim: Biological parameters such as dwelling times at states, neuronal firing rates and neuromodulation relate to the delay discounting parameter of the TD algorithm.
source: We discuss how biological parameters such as dwelling times at states, neuronal firing rates and neuromodulation relate to the delay discounting parameter of the TD algorithm, and how they influence the learned representation.
evidence: This is shown through the mathematical derivations relating gamma to biological parameters.

claim: The discount factor decreases hyperbolically with time, in agreement with psychological studies and contrary to reinforcement learning theory.
source: We also find that, in agreement with psychological studies and contrary to reinforcement learning theory, the discount factor decreases hyperbolically with time.
evidence: This is derived mathematically and discussed in the context of psychological literature on hyperbolic discounting.

claim: Replays aid learning in novel environments.
source: Finally, our framework suggests a role for replays, in both aiding learning in novel environments and finding shortcut trajectories that were not experienced during behavior, in agreement with experimental data.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations showing faster learning with replays in novel environments.

claim: Replays can find shortcut trajectories that were not experienced during behavior.
source: Finally, our framework suggests a role for replays, in both aiding learning in novel environments and finding shortcut trajectories that were not experienced during behavior, in agreement with experimental data.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation of the Wu et al. 2017 experiment where replays lead to avoidance behavior.

claim: Tolman proposed the concept of cognitive maps in the mid twentieth century.
source: Mid twentieth century, Tolman proposed the concept of cognitive maps (Tolman, 1948).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Cognitive maps are abstract mental models of an environment which are helpful when learning tasks and in decision making.
source: These maps are abstract mental models of an environment which are helpful when learning tasks and in decision making.
evidence: This is a definition from the cognitive science literature.

claim: The hippocampus can provide the substrate to encode cognitive maps.
source: Since the discovery of hippocampal place cells, cells that are activated only in specific locations of an environment, it is believed that the hippocampus can provide the substrate to encode such cognitive maps (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by the discovery of place cells and subsequent research.

claim: Place cells are activated only in specific locations of an environment.
source: Since the discovery of hippocampal place cells, cells that are activated only in specific locations of an environment, it is believed that the hippocampus can provide the substrate to encode such cognitive maps (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is the defining characteristic of place cells as discovered by O'Keefe and colleagues.

claim: The successor representation framework has computational advantages including efficient learning, simple computation of state values, fast relearning when rewards change, and flexible decision making.
source: Theoretically, this SR framework has some computational advantages, such as efficient learning, simple computation of the values of states, fast relearning when the rewards change and flexible decision making (Dayan, 1993; Stachenfeld et al., 2014; Stachenfeld et al., 2017; Russek et al., 2017; Momennejad et al., 2017).
evidence: These advantages are described in the cited theoretical work on the successor representation.

claim: The firing fields of hippocampal place cells are affected by the strategy used by the animal to navigate the environment.
source: Firstly, the firing fields of hippocampal place cells are affected by the strategy used by the animal to navigate the environment (known as the policy in machine learning), as well as by changes in the environment (Mehta et al., 2000; Stachenfeld et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an experimental observation cited from the literature.

claim: Reward revaluation would be more effective than transition revaluation.
source: Secondly, reward revaluation — the ability to recompute the values of the states when rewards change — would be more effective than transition revaluation (Russek et al., 2017; Momennejad et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the successor representation framework.

claim: The model can learn over a behavioral timescale while using STDP timescales in the millisecond range.
source: Our model can thus learn over a behavioral timescale while using STDP timescales in the millisecond range.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical analysis and simulations.

claim: The framework smoothly connects a temporally precise spiking code akin to replay activity with a rate based code akin to behavioral spiking.
source: We show mathematically that our proposed framework smoothly connects a temporally precise spiking code akin to replay activity with a rate based code akin to behavioral spiking.
evidence: This is shown through the mathematical derivations relating lambda to the timescale T.

claim: The delay-discounting in the model depends hyperbolically on time but exponentially on state transitions.
source: Moreover, the delay-discounting in our model depends hyperbolically on time but exponentially on state transitions.
evidence: This is shown through the mathematical analysis of how gamma depends on T.

claim: Replays have been speculated to be involved in learning models of the environment, supported by experiments.
source: Finally, replays have long been speculated to be involved in learning models of the environment, supported by experiments (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Kay et al., 2020) and models (Hasselmo and Eichenbaum, 2005; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Kubie and Fenton, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Replays can be used to learn offline, allowing policies to be refined without actual exploration.
source: We show how we can use replays to learn offline. In this way, policies can be refined without the need for actual exploration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation of the Wu et al. 2017 experiment.

claim: The model consists of a feedforward network of excitatory neurons with biologically plausible spike-timing dependent plasticity on the implementational level.
source: On the implementational level, our model consists of a feedforward network of excitatory neurons with biologically plausible spike-timing dependent plasticity.
evidence: This describes the neural network architecture used in the model.

claim: On the computational theory level, the model tackles representation learning using cognitive maps.
source: On the computational theory level, our model tackles representation learning using cognitive maps.
evidence: This describes the high-level computational goal of the model.

claim: The successor representation can be understood as how likely it is for the animal to visit a future location starting from its current position.
source: In this setting, the SR can be understood as how likely it is for the animal to visit a future location starting from its current position.
evidence: This is an intuitive explanation of the successor representation.

claim: The presynaptic layer represents the hippocampal CA3 region in the model.
source: Similar to McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Hasselmo and Schnell, 1994; Mehta et al., 2000; Hasselmo et al., 2002, we assume that the presynaptic layer represents the hippocampal CA3 region and is all-to-all connected to a postsynaptic layer - representing the CA1 network (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an assumption of the model based on previous work.

claim: The postsynaptic layer represents the CA1 network in the model.
source: Similar to McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Hasselmo and Schnell, 1994; Mehta et al., 2000; Hasselmo et al., 2002, we assume that the presynaptic layer represents the hippocampal CA3 region and is all-to-all connected to a postsynaptic layer - representing the CA1 network (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an assumption of the model based on previous work.

claim: The synaptic connections from CA3 to CA1 are plastic and follow a spike-timing-dependent plasticity rule.
source: The synaptic connections from CA3 to CA1 are plastic such that the weight changes follow a spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) rule consisting of two terms: a weight-dependent depression term for presynaptic spikes and a potentiation term for pre-post spike pairs (Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes the plasticity mechanism in the model.

claim: Using the spike-timing dependent plasticity rule, the SR is learned in the synaptic weights.
source: These activations subsequently trigger plasticity at the synapses, and we can show analytically that, using the spike-timing dependent plasticity rule discussed above, the SR is learned in the synaptic weights (Figure 1e and f, and see Appendix).
evidence: This is proven analytically in the Appendix and demonstrated in simulations.

claim: The framework combines learning based on rate coding as well as temporal coding.
source: This framework therefore combines learning based on rate coding as well as temporal coding.
evidence: This follows from the smooth transition between different values of lambda corresponding to different timescales.

claim: The strategy of using replays to learn is in line with recent experimental and theoretical observations.
source: This strategy of using replays to learn is in line with recent experimental and theoretical observations (see Momennejad, 2020 for a review).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The noise from random spike times can be mitigated by averaging over a population of neurons.
source: This noise can be mitigated by averaging over a population of neurons.
evidence: This is a standard approach in computational neuroscience.

claim: Weights between neurons encoding positions that are behaviorally far apart can be learnt using a learning rule on a synaptic timescale.
source: Eventually, weights between neurons encoding positions that are behaviorally far apart can be learnt using a learning rule on a synaptic timescale (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the bootstrapping mechanism.

claim: The TD(0) algorithm relies on a property called bootstrapping.
source: From a reinforcement learning perspective, the TD(0) algorithm relies on a property called bootstrapping.
evidence: This is a standard property of TD learning algorithms.

claim: Bootstrapping means that the successor representation is learned by first taking an initial estimate of the SR matrix and then gradually adjusting this estimate by comparing it to the states the animal actually visits.
source: This means that the successor representation is learned by first taking an initial estimate of the SR matrix (i.e. the previously learned weights), and then gradually adjusting this estimate (i.e. the synaptic weights) by comparing it to the states in the environment that the animal actually visits.
evidence: This is the definition of bootstrapping in the context of TD learning.

claim: The comparison in bootstrapping is achieved by calculating a prediction error, similar to the one for dopamine neurons.
source: This comparison is achieved by calculating a prediction error, similar to the widely studied one for dopamine neurons (Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This draws an analogy to the well-known dopamine prediction error.

claim: The prediction error is computed between the predicted and observed trajectories.
source: Since the synaptic connections carry information about the expected trajectories, in this case, the prediction error is computed between the predicted and observed trajectories (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is explained in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Bootstrapping allows learning over long timescales using synaptic plasticity alone.
source: The main point of bootstrapping, therefore, is that learning happens by adjusting our current predictions (e.g. synaptic weights) to match the observed current state. This information is available at each time step and thus allows learning over long timescales using synaptic plasticity alone.
evidence: This is the key insight explaining how behavioral timescale learning is possible with millisecond plasticity.

claim: The prediction error in the model is not encoded by a separate mechanism like dopamine.
source: It is important to notice that the prediction error in our model is not encoded by a separate mechanism in the way that dopamine is thought to do for reward prediction (Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This distinguishes the model from dopamine-based reward prediction error models.

claim: The prediction error is represented locally at the level of the synapse through the depression and potentiation terms of the STDP rule.
source: Instead, the prediction error is represented locally, at the level of the synapse, through the depression and potentiation terms of our STDP rule, and the current weight encodes the current estimate of the SR (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis of the STDP rule.

claim: The model does not need an external vector to carry prediction error signals as proposed in Gardner et al., 2018; Gershman, 2018.
source: We therefore do not need an external vector to carry prediction error signals as proposed in Gardner et al., 2018; Gershman, 2018.
evidence: This distinguishes the model from other approaches.

claim: The synaptic potentiation updates a row of the SR, while the synaptic depression updates a column.
source: In fact, the synaptic potentiation in our model updates a row of the SR, while the synaptic depression updates a column.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis of the STDP rule.

claim: For very fast timescales such as replays, TD(1) is equivalent to online Monte Carlo learning.
source: On the other extreme, for very fast timescales such as replays, TD(1) is equivalent to online Monte Carlo learning (MC), which does not bootstrap at all.
evidence: This is a standard result from reinforcement learning theory.

claim: Monte Carlo samples the whole trajectory and then takes the average of the discounted state occupancies to update the SR.
source: Instead, MC samples the whole trajectory and then simply takes the average of the discounted state occupancies to update the SR (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is the definition of Monte Carlo learning.

claim: During replays, the whole trajectory falls under the plasticity window and the network can learn without bootstrapping.
source: During replays, the whole trajectory falls under the plasticity window and the network can learn without bootstrapping.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis for fast timescales.

claim: Synaptic plasticity leads to the development of a successor representation in which synaptic weights can be directly linked to the successor matrix.
source: In summary, in our framework, synaptic plasticity leads to the development of a successor representation in which synaptic weights can be directly linked to the successor matrix.
evidence: This is the main result of the model.

claim: In reinforcement learning, it is usual to have delay-discounting where rewards that are further away in the future are discounted compared to rewards in the immediate future.
source: In reinforcement learning, it is usual to have delay-discounting: rewards that are further away in the future are discounted compared to rewards that are in the immediate future.
evidence: This is a standard concept in reinforcement learning.

claim: The usual approach to use exponential discount when time is continuous is to discretize time by choosing a unit of time.
source: In order to still use the above exponential discount when time is continuous, the usual approach is to discretize time by choosing a unit of time.
evidence: This is the standard approach in continuous-time RL.

claim: The dependence of γ on T can be interpreted as an increased discounting the longer a state lasts.
source: The dependence on T can be interpreted as an increased discounting the longer a state lasts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical relationship.

claim: The framework allows the agent to act in continuous time.
source: This allows the agent to act in continuous time (Figure 3c and e).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations.

claim: The difference between hyperbolic and exponential discount is that we attribute a different value to the same temporal delay depending on whether it happens sooner or later.
source: The difference between a hyperbolic discount and an exponential discount lays in the fact that we will attribute a different value to the same temporal delay, depending on whether it happens sooner or later.
evidence: This is the defining characteristic of hyperbolic discounting.

claim: People tend to prefer 100 dollars today instead of 101 dollars tomorrow, while they tend to prefer 101 dollars in 31 days instead of 100 dollars in 30 days.
source: A classic example is that, when given the choice, people tend to prefer 100 dollars today instead of 101 dollars tomorrow, while they tend to prefer 101 dollars in 31 days instead of 100 dollars in 30 days.
evidence: This is a classic example from behavioral economics illustrating hyperbolic discounting.

claim: Exponential discounting always attributes the same value to the same delay no matter when it occurs.
source: Exponential discounting, on the other hand, always attributes the same value to the same delay no matter when it occurs.
evidence: This is the defining characteristic of exponential discounting.

claim: The model combines two types of discounting: exponential when moving through space and hyperbolic when moving through time.
source: Our model therefore combines two types of discounting: exponential when we move through space — when sequentially activating different place cells — and hyperbolic when we move through time — when we prolong the activity of the same place cell.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: State-dependent discounting can be useful to encode salient locations in the environment such as landmarks or reward locations.
source: Such state-dependent discounting can be useful to for example encode salient locations in the environment such as landmarks or reward locations (Figure 3c and f).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations.

claim: The MC algorithm presents low bias.
source: As such, the estimated SR matrix will be a close approximation of the theoretical value. The difference between the estimated and theoretical value is commonly referred to as bias. We can therefore say that the MC algorithm presents low bias.
evidence: This is a standard property of Monte Carlo methods.

claim: The MC estimate has high variance when the agent moves randomly.
source: However, if the agent moves in the environment at random, the sampled trajectories will be quite different from each other. When taking the average, the estimated value will therefore fluctuate a lot. In this case, we say that the MC estimate has high variance as well (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a standard property of Monte Carlo methods and demonstrated in simulations.

claim: The TD algorithm presents high bias and low variance.
source: The TD algorithm therefore presents high bias and low variance.
evidence: This is a standard property of TD methods.

claim: Replays should initially speed up learning in an unfamiliar environment because the MC algorithm is unbiased by the initial estimate of the SR.
source: Since the MC algorithm is unbiased by the initial estimate of the SR, replays should initially speed up learning in an unfamiliar environment.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the bias-variance properties of MC.

claim: When the environment becomes familiar, the TD algorithm will be preferred because we prefer to have low variance.
source: Later on, when the environment becomes familiar, the SR estimate is already closer to the exact value. At this point, we prefer to have low variance and thus the TD algorithm will be preferred.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the bias-variance properties of TD.

claim: Having proportionally more replays at the first trials in a novel environment leads to both quick learning and low error at convergence.
source: We confirm this logic using our spiking neural networks, and show how we can have both quick learning and low error at convergence if we proportionally have more replays at the first trials in a novel environment (Figure 4a–e).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations.

claim: Having an equal proportion of replays throughout the whole simulation does not yield as quick learning as MC and as low asymptotic error as TD.
source: In contrast, when having an equal proportion of replays throughout the whole simulation, we do not yield as quick learning as MC and as low asymptotic error as TD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations.

claim: The pattern of proportionally more replays in novel environments versus familiar environments has been experimentally observed.
source: Interestingly, the pattern of proportionally more replays in novel environments versus familiar environments has also been experimentally observed (Cheng and Frank, 2008; Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental data.

claim: In the Wu et al., 2017 experiment, rats were allowed to freely explore a linear track on day 1, with half the track dark and half bright.
source: For this purpose, we reproduce an place-avoidance experiment from Wu et al., 2017. In short, rats are allowed to freely explore a linear track on day 1. Half of the track is dark, while the other half is bright.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol from the cited study.

claim: In the Wu et al., 2017 experiment, animals received two mild footshocks when entering the shock zone in the second trial.
source: On day 2, the animals did four trials separated by resting periods: in the first trial (pre), the animals were free to explore the track; in the second trial (shock), they started in the light zone and received two mild footshocks when entering in the shock zone; in the third and fourth trial (post and re-exposure, respectively), they were allowed to freely explore the track again, but starting from the light zone or the shock zone respectively (Figure 5a).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol from the cited study.

claim: In the Wu et al., 2017 study, during the post trial, animals tended to stay in the light zone and forward replays from the current position to the shock zone were observed when animals reached the boundary between light and dark zones.
source: In the study, it was reported that during the post trial, animals tended to stay in the light zone and forward replays from the current position to the shock zone were observed when the animals reached the boundary between the light and the dark zone (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: This describes experimental observations from the cited study.

claim: In the simulation without replays, the agent keeps extensively exploring the dark zone even after experiencing the shock.
source: Left: without replays, the agent keeps extensively exploring the dark zone even after having experienced the shock.
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 5d.

claim: In the simulation with replays, the agent largely avoids entering the dark zone after experiencing the shock.
source: Right: with replays, the agent largely avoids entering the dark zone after having experienced the shock (replays not shown).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 5d.

claim: The replays affect the learning of the successor representation and the negative reward information is propagated towards the decision point.
source: The replays affect the learning of the successor representation and the negative reward information is propagated towards the decision point in the middle of the track.
evidence: This is the mechanism by which replays affect behavior in the simulation.

claim: The states in the dark zone have lower value with replays compared to the case without replays.
source: The states in the dark zone therefore have lower value compared to the case without replays (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results.

claim: Even when doubling the amount of SR updates in the scenario without replays, the behavior of the agent remains unaltered.
source: Moreover, even when doubling the amount of SR updates in the scenario without replays, the behavior of the agent remains unaltered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary simulations.

claim: It is the type of policy and not the amount of updates that leads to the different behavior.
source: This shows that it is not the amount of updates, but the type of policy that is important when updating the SR, and how using a different policy in the replay activity can significantly alter behavior.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the supplementary simulations.

claim: The simulation setup is simplified and does not aim to reproduce the complex decision making of the rats.
source: Our setup for this simulation is simplified, and does not aim to reproduce the complex decision making of the rats.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the simulation.

claim: Replaying trajectories that were not directly experienced before can substantially influence the final policy of an agent and overall performance.
source: Nonetheless, it is interesting to see how replaying trajectories that were not directly experienced before, in combination with a model allowing replays to affect the learning of a cognitive map, can substantially influence the final policy of an agent and the overall performance.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the Wu et al. simulation.

claim: While the model suggests a potential role for the SR in solving the Wu et al. task, the data would also be compatible with a model-based strategy.
source: It is important to note here that, while we are suggesting a potential role for the SR in solving this task, the data itself would also be compatible with a model-based strategy.
evidence: This acknowledges alternative explanations for the experimental data.

claim: Experimental evidence suggests that humans may use a mixed strategy involving both model-based reinforcement learning and the successor representation.
source: In fact, experimental evidence suggests that humans may use a mixed strategy involving both model-based reinforcement learning and the successor representation (Momennejad et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental evidence.

claim: The network learns the SR in the CA3-CA1 weights.
source: Our network learns the SR in the CA3-CA1 weights.
evidence: This is shown through mathematical analysis and simulations.

claim: The firing rate is proportional to the total synaptic weights because neurons integrate synaptic EPSPs and generate spikes using an inhomogeneous Poisson process based on depolarization.
source: Since we have modeled neurons to integrate the synaptic EPSPs and generate spikes using an inhomogeneous Poisson process based on the depolarization, the firing rate is proportional to the total synaptic weights.
evidence: This follows from the neuron model used.

claim: The successor representation can be read out simply by a downstream neuron.
source: Therefore, the successor representation can be read out simply by a downstream neuron.
evidence: This follows from the proportionality between firing rate and synaptic weights.

claim: The value of a state is defined by the inner product between the successor matrix and the reward vector.
source: Moreover, since the value of a state is defined by the inner product between the successor matrix and the reward vector, it is sufficient for the synaptic weights to the downstream neuron to learn the reward vector, and the downstream neuron will then encode the state value in its firing rate (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is the standard definition of value in the successor representation framework.

claim: During learning, both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic layers receive external inputs representing the current state.
source: It is worth noting that, during learning, both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic layers receive external inputs representing the current state (Equation 10 and Equation 11 in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is part of the model specification.

claim: The external inputs may induce a distortion in the read out of the diagonal elements of the SR matrix.
source: This may induce a distortion in the read out of the diagonal elements of the SR matrix (see Equations 13 and 15, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the mathematical analysis and supplementary figures.

claim: There are multiple ways to resolve the apparent conflict between learning and reading out.
source: However, there are multiple ways we could resolve this apparent conflict:
evidence: The authors propose several potential solutions.

claim: The external current in CA1 is present for only a fraction of the time T in each state, so readout might happen during the period of CA3 activation exclusively.
source: (i) Since the external current in CA1 is present for only a fraction of the time T in each state, the readout might happen during the period of CA3 activation exclusively;
evidence: This is one proposed solution to the learning-readout conflict.

claim: The readout may be over the whole time T but becomes more noisy towards the end, with distortion limited to diagonal elements.
source: (ii) The readout may be over the whole time T but becomes more noisy towards the end. Even in the case where the readout is noisy, the distortion would be limited to the diagonal elements of the matrix;
evidence: This is another proposed solution.

claim: Learning and readout may be separate mechanisms, where the CA3 driving current is present during readout only, possibly signaled by neuromodulation.
source: (iii) Learning and readout may be separate mechanisms, where the CA3 driving current is present during readout only. This could be for instance signaled by neuromodulation (e.g. noradrenaline and acetylcholine are active during learning but not exploration Micheau and Marighetto, 2011; Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Robbins, 1997; Teles-Grilo Ruivo and Mellor, 2013; Palacios-Filardo et al., 2021), or it could be that readout happens during replays;
evidence: This is another proposed solution with supporting citations.

claim: The weights to or activation functions of the readout neuron may learn to compensate for the distorted signal in CA1.
source: (iv) The weights to or activation functions of the readout neuron may learn to compensate for the distorted signal in CA1.
evidence: This is another proposed solution.

claim: The external inputs encoding the current state activate CA3 first, and CA1 later.
source: Furthermore, we can notice that the external inputs encoding the current state activate CA3 first, and CA1 later.
evidence: This is part of the model specification.

claim: Similar learning rules to the one proposed have been observed in the hippocampus.
source: Similar learning rules have indeed been observed in the hippocampus (Shouval et al., 2002 and proposed on theoretical grounds Mehta et al., 2000; Waddington et al., 2012; van Rossum et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental and theoretical work.

claim: The TD algorithm is most commonly known in neuroscience for describing how reward prediction can be computed in the brain.
source: The TD algorithm is most commonly known in neuroscience for describing how reward prediction can be computed in the brain.
evidence: This is common knowledge in computational neuroscience.

claim: It is widely believed that dopamine neurons in the VTA and SNc encode the prediction error between observed and expected reward.
source: More specifically, it is widely believed that dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra (SNc) encode the prediction error between the observed and expected reward (Schultz et al., 1997), dopamine thus acts as a global signal that can be broadcasted to other areas of the brain like the striatum to compute the expected reward.
evidence: This is a well-established theory in neuroscience.

claim: In the model, the TD algorithm estimates the SR (expected future occupancy) rather than the value.
source: In our model, the TD algorithm estimates the SR (i.e. expected future occupancy), rather than the value.
evidence: This distinguishes the model from reward prediction error models.

claim: The prediction error for the SR is different for every synaptic connection, so it's not clear how it could be carried by a global signal analogous to dopamine.
source: However, since the prediction error for the SR is different for every synaptic connection (i.e. each pair of states), it is not clear how it could be carried by a global signal analogous to dopamine.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the difference between SR and value learning.

claim: The SR would need multiple signals or a matrix transformation of the global signal.
source: The SR would need multiple signals, or a matrix transformation of the global signal.
evidence: This follows from the previous claim about the need for different prediction errors.

claim: Thanks to presynaptic depression, the STDP rule alone allows computation of negative prediction errors.
source: Furthermore, thanks to the presynaptic depression, our STDP rule alone allows us to compute negative prediction errors, which still poses an open challenge for computation with dopamine because of the low baseline dopaminergic firing rate (Glimcher, 2011; Daw et al., 2002; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007).
evidence: This is an advantage of the model over dopamine-based models.

claim: The framework smoothly connects a temporally precise spiking code with a fully rate-based code, and anything in between.
source: Our framework smoothly connects a temporally precise spiking code with a fully rate-based code, and anything in between.
evidence: This is shown through the mathematical analysis.

claim: Fast spiking sequences (temporal code) can be used for consolidation of previous experiences using Monte Carlo learning.
source: Fast spiking sequences (temporal code) can be used for consolidation of previous experiences using Monte Carlo learning, while the behavioral timescale activity (rate code) results in TD updates, allowing learning on the timescale of seconds even with plasticity timeconstants on the order of milliseconds.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Behavioral timescale activity (rate code) results in TD updates, allowing learning on the timescale of seconds even with plasticity timeconstants on the order of milliseconds.
source: Fast spiking sequences (temporal code) can be used for consolidation of previous experiences using Monte Carlo learning, while the behavioral timescale activity (rate code) results in TD updates, allowing learning on the timescale of seconds even with plasticity timeconstants on the order of milliseconds.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: This type of Hebbian learning over behavioral timescale is different than the one-shot behavioral plasticity described in Bittner et al., 2017.
source: This type of Hebbian learning over behavioral timescale exploits the bootstrapping property of TD, and is different than the one-shot behavioral plasticity described in Bittner et al., 2017.
evidence: This distinguishes the model from other approaches.

claim: The two mechanisms (this model and Bittner et al. 2017) could be complementary, where the latter plays a role in formation of new place fields while the former shapes existing place fields to contain predictive information.
source: However, these two mechanisms could be complementary, where the latter could play a more significant role in the formation of new place fields, while the former would be more relevant to shape the existing place fields to contain predictive information.
evidence: This is speculation about how different mechanisms might work together.

claim: Learning on behavioral timescales using STDP was also investigated in Drew and Abbott, 2006.
source: Learning on behavioral timescales using STDP was also investigated in Drew and Abbott, 2006.
evidence: This cites related work.

claim: The main difference between Drew and Abbott, 2006 and this work is that the former relies on overlapping neural activity from the start, while this model does not require such overlap.
source: The main difference between Drew and Abbott, 2006 and our work, is that the former relies on overlapping neural activity between the pre- and post-synaptic neurons from the start, while in our case no such overlap is required.
evidence: This distinguishes the model from related work.

claim: The setup allows learning connections between a presynaptic neuron and a postsynaptic neuron whose activities are separated by behavioral timescales initially.
source: In other words, our setup allows us to learn connections between a presynaptic neuron and a postsynaptic neuron whose activities are separated by behavioral timescales initially.
evidence: This is a key feature of the model.

claim: For learning connections separated by behavioral timescales, the task needs to be repeated many times and a chain of neurons must be consecutively activated between the presynaptic and postsynaptic neuron.
source: For this to be possible, there are two requirements: (1) the task needs to be repeated many times and (2) a chain of neurons are consecutively activated between the aforementioned presynaptic and postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: These are the requirements for the bootstrapping mechanism to work.

claim: Due to the chain of neurons, over time the activity of the postsynaptic neuron will start earlier, eventually overlapping with the presynaptic neuron.
source: Due to this chain of neurons, over time the activity of the postsynaptic neuron will start earlier, eventually overlapping with the presynaptic neuron.
evidence: This explains how the bootstrapping mechanism leads to learning.

claim: The work did not include theta modulation.
source: In our work, we did not include theta modulation, but phase precession and theta sequences could be yet another type of activity within the TD lambda framework.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and suggests future directions.

claim: A recent work (George et al., 2023) incorporated theta sweeps into behavioral activity, showing it approximately learns the SR.
source: A recent work (George et al., 2023) incorporated the theta sweeps into behavioral activity, showing it approximately learns the SR.
evidence: This cites related recent work.

claim: Theta sequences allow for fast learning, playing a similar role as replays in this work.
source: Moreover, theta sequences allow for fast learning, playing a similar role as replays (or any other fast temporal-code sequences) in our work.
evidence: This draws a connection between theta sequences and replays.

claim: By simulating temporally compressed and precise theta sequences, the George et al. model also reconciles learning over behavioral timescales with STDP.
source: By simulating the temporally compressed and precise theta sequences, their model also reconciles the learning over behavioral timescales with STDP.
evidence: This describes a similarity with related work.

claim: This framework reconciles both timescales relying purely on rate-coding during behavior, in contrast to the George et al. approach.
source: In contrast, our framework reconciles both timescales relying purely on rate-coding during behavior.
evidence: This distinguishes the model from related work.

claim: The George et al. method allows learning the SR within continuous space.
source: Finally, their method allows to learn the SR within continuous space.
evidence: This describes a feature of related work.

claim: It would be interesting to investigate whether these methods (this work and George et al.) co-exist in the hippocampus and other brain areas.
source: It would be interesting to investigate whether these methods co-exist in the hippocampus and other brain areas.
evidence: This suggests a future research direction.

claim: Fang et al., 2023 recently showed how the SR can be learned using recurrent neural networks with biologically plausible plasticity.
source: Furthermore, (Fang et al., 2023) et al. recently showed how the SR can be learned using recurrent neural networks with biologically plausible plasticity.
evidence: This cites related recent work.

claim: There are three different neural activities in the proposed framework: the presynaptic layer (CA3), the postsynaptic layer (CA1), and the external inputs.
source: There are three different neural activities in our proposed framework: the presynaptic layer (CA3), the postsynaptic layer (CA1), and the external inputs.
evidence: This describes the components of the model.

claim: The external inputs could be location-dependent currents from the entorhinal cortex, with timings guided by theta oscillations.
source: These external inputs could for example be location-dependent currents from the entorhinal cortex, with timings guided by the theta oscillations.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological source of external inputs.

claim: The dependence of CA1 place fields on CA3 and entorhinal input is in line with lesion studies.
source: The dependence of CA1 place fields on CA3 and entorhinal input is in line with lesion studies (see e.g. Brun et al., 2008; Hales et al., 2014; O'Reilly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: It would be interesting for future studies to further dissect the role various areas play in learning cognitive maps.
source: It would be interesting for future studies to further dissect the role various areas play in learning cognitive maps.
evidence: This suggests a future research direction.

claim: The SR does not require predictive information to come from higher-level feedback inputs.
source: Notably, even though we have focused on the hippocampus in our work, the SR does not require predictive information to come from higher-level feedback inputs.
evidence: This is a property of the SR framework.

claim: The framework could be useful even in sensory areas where certain stimuli are usually followed by other stimuli, creating sequences whose temporal structure can be encoded.
source: This framework could therefore be useful even in sensory areas: certain stimuli are usually followed by other stimuli, essentially creating a sequence of states whose temporal structure can be encoded in the network using our framework.
evidence: This is speculation about broader applicability of the framework.

claim: Replays have been observed in other brain areas besides the hippocampus.
source: Interestingly, replays have been observed in other brain areas besides the hippocampus (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016; Staresina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: Temporal difference learning has been proposed in the past as a way to implement prospective coding.
source: Furthermore, temporal difference learning in itself has been proposed in the past as a way to implement prospective coding (Brea et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites related theoretical work.

claim: A role for replays in learning the SR has been proposed, in line with experimental findings and RL theories.
source: We have also proposed a role for replays in learning the SR, in line with experimental findings and RL theories (Russek et al., 2017; Momennejad et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Replays are thought to serve different functions, spanning from consolidation to planning.
source: In general, replays are thought to serve different functions, spanning from consolidation to planning (Roscow et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: When replayed trajectories are similar to those observed during behavior, they speed up and consolidate learning by regulating the bias-variance trade-off, especially useful in novel environments.
source: Here, we have shown that when the replayed trajectories are similar to the ones observed during behavior, they play the role of speeding up and consolidating learning by regulating the bias-variance trade-off, which is especially useful in novel environments.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations.

claim: If replayed trajectories differ from those experienced during wakefulness, replays can play a role in reshaping the representation of space, suggesting involvement in planning.
source: On the other hand, if the replayed trajectories differ from the ones experienced during wakefulness, replays can play a role in reshaping the representation of space, which would suggest their involvement in planning.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the Wu et al. simulation.

claim: Experimentally, replays often start and end from relevant locations in the environment, like reward sites, decision points, obstacles or the current position of the animal.
source: Experimentally, it has been observed that replays often start and end from relevant locations in the environment, like reward sites, decision points, obstacles or the current position of the animal (Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Jackson et al., 2006; Mattar and Daw, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: The observation that replays start and end from salient locations is in line with the proposition that replays can be used to maintain a convenient representation of the environment.
source: Since these are salient locations, it is in line with our proposition that replays can be used to maintain a convenient representation of the environment.
evidence: This connects experimental observations to the model's predictions.

claim: Replays can serve a variety of functions, and the framework proposes additional beneficial properties without claiming to explain all observed replays.
source: It is worth noticing that replays can serve a variety of functions, and our framework merely proposes additional beneficial properties without claiming to explain all observed replays.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the model.

claim: In addition to forward replays, reverse replays are also ubiquitous in hippocampus.
source: For example, in addition to forward replays, also reverse replays are ubiquitous in hippocampus (Pfeiffer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Indirect evidence supports the idea that replays can play a role during learning.
source: Moreover, while indirect evidence supports the idea that replays can play a role during learning (Igata et al., 2021), it is not yet clear how synaptic plasticity is manifested during replays (Fuchsberger and Paulsen, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: It is not yet clear how synaptic plasticity is manifested during replays.
source: Moreover, while indirect evidence supports the idea that replays can play a role during learning (Igata et al., 2021), it is not yet clear how synaptic plasticity is manifested during replays (Fuchsberger and Paulsen, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Time and space can be discounted differently in the model.
source: We propose in our work that time and space can be discounted differently.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The flexibility to change the discounting factor by modulating firing rates and plasticity parameters suggests these mechanisms could be used to encode a variety of information in a cognitive map.
source: Moreover, the flexibility to change the discounting factor by modulating firing rates and plasticity parameters — which is ubiquitous in neural circuits — suggests that these mechanisms could be used to encode a variety of information in a cognitive map.
evidence: This is an implication of the model's properties.

claim: The specific dependence of the discount factor on biological parameters leads to experimentally testable predictions.
source: Moreover, the specific dependence of the discount factor on the biological parameters leads to experimentally testable predictions.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's predictive power.

claim: The framework predicts well-defined changes in place fields after modulations of firing rates, speed of the agent or neuromodulation of the plasticity parameters.
source: Indeed, our framework predicts well-defined changes in place fields after modulations of firing rates, speed of the agent or neuromodulation of the plasticity parameters (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations.

claim: The discount parameter depends on the time spent in each state, eliminating the need for time discretization.
source: Importantly, the discount parameter also depends on the time spent in each state. This eliminates the need for time discretization, which does not reflect the continuous nature of the response of time cells (Kraus et al., 2013).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis and supported by citation.

claim: RL agents that only use spatial data do not provide complete descriptions of behavior, which likely arises from integrating information across multiple sensory inputs.
source: For example, RL agents that only use spatial data do not provide complete descriptions of behavior, which likely arises from integrating information across multiple sensory inputs.
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the RL framework.

claim: An animal would be able to smell and see a reward from a certain distance, whereas an agent exploring the environment would only discover it when randomly visiting the exact reward location.
source: Whereas an animal would be able to smell and see a reward from a certain distance, an agent exploring the environment would only be able to discover it when randomly visiting the exact reward location.
evidence: This illustrates a limitation of spatial-only RL agents.

claim: The RL framework rests on fairly strict mathematical assumptions: the state space needs to be markovian, time and space need to be discretized, and the discounting needs to follow an exponential decay.
source: Furthermore, the framework rests on fairly strict mathematical assumptions: typically the state space needs to be markovian, time and space need to be discretized (which we manage to evade in this particular framework) and the discounting needs to follow an exponential decay.
evidence: These are standard assumptions in RL.

claim: The assumptions of RL are simplistic and it is not clear how often they are actually met.
source: These assumptions are simplistic and it is not clear how often they are actually met.
evidence: This is a critique of the RL framework.

claim: Reinforcement Learning is a sample-intensive technique, whereas some animals including humans are capable of much faster or even one-shot learning.
source: Reinforcement Learning is also a sample-intensive technique, whereas we know that some animals, including humans, are capable of much faster or even one-shot learning.
evidence: This is a known limitation of RL compared to biological learning.

claim: The whole action selection process is still computed only at the algorithmic level, even though a neural implementation of the SR and value function is provided.
source: Even though we have provided a neural implementation of the SR, and of the value function as its read-out (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2), the whole action selection process is still computed only at the algorithmic level.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the model.

claim: It may be interesting to extend the neural implementation to the policy selection mechanism in the future.
source: It may be interesting to extend the neural implementation to the policy selection mechanism in the future.
evidence: This suggests a future research direction.

claim: The work joins a variety of concepts from the neuronal level over cognitive theories to reinforcement learning in a single framework.
source: Taken together, our work joins — in a single framework — a variety of concepts from the neuronal level over cognitive theories to reinforcement learning.
evidence: This summarizes the scope and contribution of the work.
